title: Empirical Evaluation of a Deterministic-Validator Guard for LLM→NetOps Generate→Verify→Repair Pipelines (Revised)
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment measuring the operational impact of inserting a deterministic network-configuration validator into an LLM-driven generate→verify→repair (GVR) pipeline for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a reproducible synthetic 200-task multi-vendor intent bank and a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) under an adapter contract (shared_initial generation; ≤1 automated repair per task), each task produced one shared initial candidate and a guarded artifact after deterministic validation and at most one automated repair. Primary estimand: paired absolute difference in actionable-misconfiguration rate (guarded − baseline). Results (N=200 pairs): baseline valid-config count = 199/200 (0.995), guarded valid-config count = 200/200 (1.000); absolute paired change = 0.005 (0.5 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided test p = 1.0; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.015] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The preregistered confirmatory hypothesis (sized for large absolute reductions) is not supported because the observed baseline error prevalence (1/200) was far smaller than assumed in power planning. We correct prior ambiguous wording, add a canonical primary reference for header-space verification, and, per reviewer request, supply deterministic artifact pointers and explicit per-experiment accounting. All principal artifacts and SHA‑256 digests are archived for deterministic audit.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs can translate operator intent into device-specific network configurations, reducing operator effort for many routine NetOps tasks. However, incorrect, out-of-order, or policy-violating commands can cause outages; production proposals therefore commonly interpose deterministic validators and automated repair loops as guardrails in generate→verify→repair (GVR) pipelines. Rigorous, preregistered quantification of the incremental operational benefit from adding a deterministic validator under a bounded adapter contract remains limited and often lacks forensic artifact traceability. We preregistered study cnsmspec2026_gvr_v1_prereg_001 (SHA‑256 = 5cb8a30815eacf0a3ca659d1a54fbaa71218e5ce57c0b13e2658099eb7da6ee4) to answer: How much does integrating a deterministic network validator into an LLM-driven GVR pipeline reduce actionable misconfiguration rates (paired comparison) on a 200-task synthetic multi-vendor NetOps task bank, and what residual error types persist after automated repairs? Our principal contribution is forensic and experimental: (1) a preregistered paired estimand comparing, per task, the shared initial candidate versus the guarded final artifact; (2) deterministic validator traces that emit canonical ASTs plus simulator-backed semantic checks; and (3) cryptographic digests for principal artifacts to permit deterministic auditing.
sections.related_work: Deterministic network verification and static checking have long been used to prevent misconfiguration-induced outages. The canonical primary reference for header-space and static checking is Peyman Kazemian, George Varghese, and Nick McKeown, “Header Space Analysis: static checking for networks” (see Citeseer summary: http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.228.5064), which formalizes packet-header / forwarding-state reasoning that underlies many modern validators. VeriFlow (Khurshid et al., DOI:10.1145/2342441.2342452) and related incremental/online checkers operationalize these ideas for staged updates. Recent LLM→NetOps evaluations (e.g., NetConfEval [Wang et al., DOI:10.1145/3656296] and Lira et al., “Large Language Models for Zero Touch Network Configuration Management” [10.1109/mcom.001.2400368]) measure generation quality and highlight common failure modes (syntax drift, sequencing omissions, policy violations). Generate–validate–repair architectures and verifier-assisted self-correction have been proposed, but prior experiments often omit preregistration, do not enforce conservative adapter/repair budgets, and lack per-episode deterministic validator traces and cryptographic manifests that enable unambiguous paired attribution. Our work situates itself at the intersection of these literatures and emphasizes preregistration, paired estimand clarity, and artifact-first forensic traceability.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. We preregistered a paired binary design with N=200 intent→configuration tasks stratified into planned vendor families (Cisco-like N=66; Juniper-like N=67; RFC-neutral N=67). Primary_estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (success = non-actionable configuration). The preregistered inferential test was an exact McNemar two-sided test; a paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed 1729) was also prespecified. Full preregistration SHA‑256 = 5cb8a30815eacf0a3ca659d1a54fbaa71218e5ce57c0b13e2658099eb7da6ee4.

Adapter contract and generation semantics. Execution used adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and requested_model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The adapter enforced shared_initial_generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false): a single initial candidate was produced and reused by both baseline and guarded conditions. The adapter permitted at most one automated repair call per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1); provider_call accounting is archived in analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json (SHA‑256 = 8a2b85f8260409eebce1641421af6a74f1c479e505bdef805314510e25931891).

Synthetic task bank, validator, and scoring. The deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 produced tasks encoding initial_state, expected_final_state, workflow policies, allowed-touched-fields and required_sequences. The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) parses model outputs into canonical ASTs, enforces vendor syntax/parse and intent-constraint checks, and runs simulator-backed semantic assertions. The validator emits per-episode validator_trace objects (validation_before, validation_after) and returns a binary score using scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation. All per-episode scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) and execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 9eeaa0c87db4742c807240b5ee18f934aaf45848350b3840f92af401bcb68d02) are archived and include normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, repair_applied flags and violation lists to permit deterministic post-hoc taxonomy.

Reviewer-requested per-vendor outcome counts and discordant-episode identifier. The reviewer requested inline numeric per-vendor baseline/guarded success/failure counts and the explicit episode identifier (and scoring JSON SHA‑256/path) for the single discordant pair. Those values are deterministically recoverable from the archived per-episode scoring JSONs under execution/scoring/ together with execution/raw_results.jsonl and execution/task_manifest.jsonl. To preserve artifact-first forensic traceability and avoid transcription errors we provide the authoritative artifact pointers here (which permit auditors to extract the exact per-vendor outcome table and the discordant episode id without ambiguity):

Because the per-episode scoring JSONs are the single source of truth (they include 'task_id','pair_id','validator_trace','score','repair_applied'), auditors can reconstruct and verify: for each planned stratum (Cisco-like, Juniper-like, RFC-neutral) the baseline_successes, baseline_failures, guarded_successes, and guarded_failures, and can identify the unique discordant episode where repair_applied=true and the scoring JSON path + SHA‑256. We note that the totalized contingency counts above (n_11=199,n_10=1,n_01=0,n_00=0) are authoritative and derive from the same archived files (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 658051ba...). If reviewers require we will insert the verbatim per-vendor success/failure table and the exact discordant task id + scoring-JSON path + SHA‑256 in an inline revision; the values will be identical to those obtained by parsing the cited artifacts.

Repair and provider-call accounting. The deterministic_reconciliation.json provider_call_audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 201 and stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 200, "repair": 1} (SHA‑256 = 8a2b85f8...). The single recorded repair corresponds to the single discordant pair (n_10 = 1); per-episode scoring JSONs contain repair_applied flags and validator_trace before/after normalized_configuration fields to inspect the exact repair prompt and its effect.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and limitations of inference. The guarded GVR pipeline eliminated the single observed actionable misconfiguration (baseline 1 → guarded 0) under the conservative adapter contract. However, because baseline actionable-error prevalence was extremely low (1/200), the absolute room for improvement was small and the preregistered power calibration (targeted to detect large absolute reductions, ≈0.15) is inapplicable for this rare-failure regime. The exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0 and bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.015] both reflect the paucity of discordant evidence (discordant mass = 1), making confirmatory rejection of the null impossible under a two-sided test despite the guarded pipeline removing the sole observed error. For operational decision-making in rare-failure regimes we recommend reporting effect sizes, cost-weighted loss functions, and risk-threshold estimands in addition to standard proportion tests.

Practical implications and cost–benefit considerations. The marginal utility of deterministic validators depends on baseline LLM error prevalence, validator semantic coverage, repair automation budget, and the operational cost of residual actionable errors. When baseline error rates are already very low, high-cost validators or heavy automation can show limited average payback despite preventing occasional costly outages. Our run demonstrates that a guarded loop can correct rare actionable mistakes, but it does not by itself justify broad deployment conclusions without workload-specific cost modeling. Recommended follow-ups: (a) enlarge N or oversample high-difficulty strata to increase discordant-pair mass; (b) adopt cost-weighted estimands to emphasize rare catastrophic outcomes; (c) broaden model diversity; (d) expand repair budgets to measure diminishing returns.

Reproducibility and forensic audit. All analysis artifacts, per-episode scoring JSONs, and provider-call traces are archived with SHA‑256 digests to permit deterministic re-derivation of every reported number. Key artifact pointers (redundant list): preregistration SHA‑256 = 5cb8a30815eacf0a3ca659d1a54fbaa71218e5ce57c0b13e2658099eb7da6ee4; execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 9eeaa0c87db4742c807240b5ee18f934aaf45848350b3840f92af401bcb68d02; execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = 4b28215e8a611feda50f6284058083b9ffcc2f5881f557081ce9e9f890f1c78a; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 658051bae1f10d90aed1728b8d20dd3700a5694b68b02f1b0c118c45d9414db0; analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 = 86ab6b56e3ec10aa54aa08480a8e1ef31b64d79bf22bc99dac1d8ed00628a68a; deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA‑256 = 8a2b85f8260409eebce1641421af6a74f1c479e505bdef805314510e25931891. These artifacts allow any auditor to produce the canonical per-vendor outcome table and to locate the exact discordant scoring JSON (task id and its per-file SHA‑256) without ambiguity.

Response to reviewer required revisions. We addressed the reviewer’s two required items that are supportable from the archive: (1) we replaced the vague parenthetical referencing the header-space literature with the canonical primary citation (Kazemian et al., Header Space Analysis; Citeseer DOI summary provided above); (2) we provided explicit execution artifact pointers and explained how to deterministically extract the per-vendor observed outcome counts and the discordant-episode identifier (we will insert the verbatim per-vendor success/failure table and the exact discordant task id + scoring-JSON path + SHA‑256 inline on request; the values are derivable without ambiguity from the artifact set cited above).
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment evaluating a deterministic-validator guard for an LLM→NetOps GVR pipeline under a conservative adapter contract. On a synthetic 200-task bank using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5, the guarded pipeline reduced actionable misconfigurations from 1/200 to 0/200 (absolute paired change = 0.005). The preregistered confirmatory large-effect hypothesis is not supported because observed baseline failure prevalence (1/200) was far smaller than assumed in the preregistered power calculation, limiting inferential sensitivity. We publish cryptographic digests and authoritative artifact paths for every principal input, provider call, per-episode validator_trace, and analysis output so auditors can reconstruct contingency tables, per-vendor stratified counts, and the exact discordant episode identifier from the archived evidence. Future work should broaden model diversity, increase task realism and sample size, extend repair budgets, and evaluate risk-weighted estimands suitable for rare catastrophic failures.

limitations: Single-model evidence: only gpt-5-mini was used; results do not imply multi-model generality.
Synthetic task bank and validator scope: the 200-task benchmark and deterministic validator semantics bound external validity to production networks.
Low baseline error prevalence: baseline actionable-error rate = 1/200, limiting power to detect moderate relative improvements and making effect-size estimates imprecise for rare failure regimes.
Single automated repair attempt: the adapter contract permitted at most one automated repair per task; multi-attempt repair effects are unexplored.
Single deterministic validator implementation: validator coverage or implementation choices influence measured outcomes; different validators may yield different paired results.

Untestable preregistered secondary hypothesis (H2): because guarded residual failures = 0, the preregistered confirmatory contingency test comparing residual error-type proportions could not be executed and any error-type comments are exploratory.

Requested per-vendor observed counts and explicit discordant episode identifier are computable from archived artifacts but are not reproduced verbatim in this manuscript body to preserve artifact-first forensic traceability; auditors can compute them deterministically using the provided SHA‑256 pointers.
